title: FOMO and chasing
teaches: FOMO, the fear of missing a move, makes you chase (buy late, far past your planned entry, with more risk per share) or jump in before your signal; the cure is an entry and stop written before the open and, if you miss it, a pullback that holds a higher low or the next setup.

facts.quote: everyone has experienced some kind of fear of missing out on something.
facts.claim: FOMO is the fear of missing out, and everyone feels it.

facts.quote: And, just because others around you might be buying into these kinds of opportunities, it doesn't mean you have to.
facts.claim: Other people buying is not a reason for you to buy.

facts.quote: stick with your long-term plan and don't make investment decisions based on a fear of missing out.
facts.claim: Stick to your plan and don't let the fear of missing out make the decision.

facts.quote: It can be tempting to jump on the bandwagon and follow whatever the crowd seems to be doing.  Sometimes, however, following the crowd may lead to significant investment losses.
facts.claim: Following the crowd into a hot stock can lead to big losses.

facts.quote: Real-time discussion platforms and buy/sell indicators driven by social sentiment may lead you to make emotionally-driven or impulsive investment decisions, which can be a risky way to approach investing.
facts.claim: Social media buzz can push you into emotional, impulsive buys.

facts.quote: Never feel pressured to invest right away.
facts.claim: Never let pressure rush you into buying.

facts.quote: fraudsters pump up a company's stock price by making false and misleading statements to create a buying frenzy, and then sell shares at the pumped up price.
facts.claim: In a pump and dump, promoters whip up a buying frenzy and sell into it.

facts.quote: is the rapid rise in the price of an investment, reflecting a high degree of collective enthusiasm or exuberance regarding the investment's prospects.  This rapid rise is usually followed by a contraction in the investment's price.
facts.claim: A mania is a fast, crowd-driven run, and it is usually followed by a fall.

facts.quote: They may even tell you that the opportunity won't last long in order to pressure you into investing right away.
facts.claim: "It won't last" is a pressure tactic used to rush you.

facts.quote: Chasing the market is synonymous with herd instinct and generally involves buying in at a high price or selling at a low price after a sell-off.
facts.claim: Chasing means following the herd, usually buying at a high price.

facts.quote: chasing the market is generally used in a negative context to refer to an investor or trader who has come into a position too late to properly benefit.
facts.claim: A chase is a position taken too late to benefit properly.

facts.quote: once the internet is talking about how great an investment is, that investment has likely already been overbought and has grown more expensive.
facts.claim: By the time everyone is talking about a stock, it has likely already run.

facts.quote: Plus, it could be about to be abandoned by earlier investors who've decided to take profits.
facts.claim: Early buyers may be getting ready to sell to the late ones.

facts.quote: Perhaps the most famous of "meme stocks" was GameStop (GME). Thanks to social media hype, in January 2021, its share price rose from around $5 to about $120 in under three weeks
facts.claim: GameStop ran from about $5 to about $120 in under three weeks of January 2021 on social media hype.

facts.quote: Many of those who arrived late to the party, though, endured significant pain. After topping out at $120.75, it was trading for just $10.97 a few weeks later
facts.claim: GameStop topped at $120.75 and traded at $10.97 a few weeks later; late buyers took the pain.

facts.quote: Regret may cause a trader to get into a trade after initially missing out on it because the stock moved too fast.
facts.claim: After missing a fast move, regret pulls traders into it late.

facts.quote: This is a violation of trading discipline and often results in direct losses from security prices that are falling from peak highs.
facts.claim: That late entry breaks discipline and often buys near a peak.

facts.quote: Developing and sticking to a trading plan with trading rules and risk management practices, can provide a structured approach to investing, minimizing room for emotional decision making.
facts.claim: A plan with rules leaves less room for emotional decisions.

facts.quote: For stock trades, the trade risk is the dollar difference between the entry price and the stop-loss.
facts.claim: Risk per share is the distance from your entry down to your stop.

facts.quote: To determine the correct position size from this information, the investor simply needs to divide the account risk ($500) by the trade risk ($20). This means 25 shares can be bought ($500 / $20).
facts.claim: Shares to buy are your dollars at risk divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: Trends are identified by drawing lines, known as trendlines, that connect price action making higher highs and higher lows for an uptrend, or lower lows and lower highs for a downtrend.
facts.claim: An uptrend makes higher highs and higher lows.

facts.quote: Stop-loss orders could sit below the breakout candle or beneath the opening range low, depending on preferred risk tolerance.
facts.claim: On an opening-range break, the stop can go under the opening range low.

facts.quote: Some investors may choose to follow only a few minutes of the opening price action, while others may prefer to see an hour or more before drawing a conclusion from the opening range.
facts.claim: Traders let the open run anywhere from minutes to an hour before acting on its range.

facts.quote: Finding a good candidate does not mean a trade should be taken prematurely. Wait patiently for the stock price to make its move.
facts.claim: A good setup is not a reason to buy before it triggers.

facts.quote: Place a stop buy order slightly above the upper trend line of the handle. Order execution should only occur if the price breaks the pattern's resistance.
facts.claim: A buy stop just over the trigger level fills only if price breaks it.

facts.quote: And when it comes to missing out on a move, traders might make the mistake of trying to jump on a move after it's already happened—perhaps at the point when it's ready to reverse.
facts.claim: Missing a move tempts traders to jump in late, sometimes right before it reverses.

facts.quote: It's usually best to stick to the plan you had, using the indicators you typically rely on, and take small losses quickly rather than dragging out a losing trade.
facts.claim: Stick to your plan and take small losses quickly.

facts.quote: It can be tempting to take on more risk when prices are rising, but doing so can leave you overexposed if an unexpected reversal occurs.
facts.claim: Rising prices tempt you into more risk, which hurts if the move reverses.

facts.quote: If a trader has trouble distancing their emotions from their trading decisions, it's never a bad idea to slow down or even take a break.
facts.claim: When emotions are driving, slow down or take a break.

facts.quote: It's important to determine this process before you start investing so you aren't making spur-of-the-moment choices based on temporary market peaks or valleys.
facts.claim: Set your entries and exits in advance so you don't decide on the spur of the moment.

facts.quote: You don't want to find yourself, for instance, investing more because prices are rising and taking on more risk than you intended.
facts.claim: Buying more because prices are rising means taking more risk than you planned.

facts.quote: In short, trading plans help remove some of the emotion and guesswork from your trading decision-making.
facts.claim: A trading plan takes some of the emotion out of decisions.

facts.quote: FOMO is a feeling that something exciting is happening while you're on the sidelines, potentially sparking anxiety or an urgency that drives impulsive decisions, especially around spending.
facts.claim: FOMO is the feeling of being on the sidelines of something exciting, and its urgency drives impulsive decisions.

facts.quote: Be patient. If a trade is missed, wait for a correction to occur before putting the trade on.
facts.claim: Rhodes' rule: if you miss a trade, wait for a pullback before putting it on.

facts.quote: Buy that which is showing strength - sell that which is showing weakness.
facts.claim: Rhodes' rule: buy what is showing strength.

facts.quote: The urge "to get the money back" is extreme, and should not be given in to.
facts.claim: Rhodes' rule: don't give in to the urge to win back losses.

facts.quote: The best place to buy a market is near support levels. That support is usually a previous reaction low.
facts.claim: Murphy: the best place to buy is near support, usually a prior reaction low.

facts.quote: After a resistance peak has been broken, it will usually provide support on subsequent pullbacks.
facts.claim: Murphy: a broken resistance level usually acts as support on later pullbacks.

facts.quote: An uptrend is defined by prices that form a series of rising peaks and rising troughs (higher highs and higher lows).
facts.claim: An uptrend is a series of higher highs and higher lows.

facts.quote: The basic tenet of gap trading is to allow one hour after the market opens for the stock price to establish its range.
facts.claim: ChartSchool's gap rule: give the open an hour to set its range before trading the gap.

facts.quote: It is more important to be consistently profitable than to chase movers or enter after the crowd.
facts.claim: Consistent profits matter more than chasing movers or following the crowd in.

facts.quote: When the emotions are running high, take a breather, step back, and analyze the situation from a greater distance.
facts.claim: When emotions run high, step back before acting.

facts.quote: Why You Should Pay Close Attention To The 5% Buy Zone After A Breakout
facts.claim: IBD's buy zone runs 5% past the buy point after a breakout.

facts.quote: That depends on how far past the buy point you get in. The further beyond the buy point, the greater the risk of getting shaken out of a stock.
facts.claim: The further past the buy point you buy, the greater the risk of getting shaken out.

facts.quote: That FOMO leads to overtrading, as the fear of missing leads to the taking of marginal trades.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: FOMO leads to overtrading in marginal trades.

facts.quote: A common pattern is that win percentage goes down when the number of trades placed increases.  This is often because the additional trades are made from a FOMO mindset.
facts.claim: Steenbarger sees win rates fall as trade counts rise, often because the extra trades come from FOMO.

facts.quote: No matter how many opportunities I miss, ones always end up appearing later in the day or the next day.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: however many trades you miss, new ones keep coming.

facts.quote: The goal is not to trade every possible opportunity, but to identify the best opportunities and trade those as well as possible.
facts.claim: The goal is the best opportunities, traded well, not every opportunity.

facts.quote: My experience in trading is that, if I'm feeling FOMO, the odds are good that others are experiencing it as well.  The trade that seems obvious is often not the high percentage trade.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: if you feel FOMO, others likely do too, and the obvious trade is often not the high-percentage one.

facts.quote: he would see the market moving away from his ideal entry point and, fearful of missing out on the opportunity, he would chase the short term movement.  All too often that led to paper cut losses
facts.claim: Steenbarger's client chased moves that ran from his entry and took repeated small losses.

facts.quote: he graded himself at the end of the day purely on process grounds
facts.claim: The fix: he graded each day on his process, not on profit and loss.

facts.quote: It appears that he front-runs his setups, getting into trades before he gets proper signals.
facts.claim: FOMO can also mean buying before the setup gives its signal.

facts.quote: Instead of buying on pullbacks or selling on bounces, you chase the market higher or lower.
facts.claim: The fear of missing makes you chase instead of buying pullbacks.

facts.quote: The reasonable trader knows that it's not about taking every conceivable opportunity:  that would be impossible.  Rather, it's about limiting your risk, while taking advantage of the best opportunities
facts.claim: Nobody takes every opportunity; the job is limiting risk and taking the best ones.

facts.quote: Traders who fear missing out on a trending move and chase strength or weakness frequently get whipsawed and stopped out.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: traders who chase a trend out of FOMO often get whipsawed and stopped out.

facts.quote: But if the result of missing trades is going to be an avalanche of self-criticism, the danger is not financial risk, but the risk of feeling worse about yourself.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: missing a trade is not a financial risk; the danger is the self-criticism after.

facts.quote: Remember, not having a position is a position.
facts.claim: Rhodes: being flat is a position too.

facts.quote: The portfolio manager suffered from that common malady of FOMO: the fear of missing out on potential market moves.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: FOMO is the fear of missing out on potential market moves.

facts.quote: Default stop: the low of the day, or the prior day's low. (Owner's answer.)
facts.claim: Our default stop is the low of the day or the prior day's low.

facts.quote: over previous day high or on day 1 kicker ORB on the 30 minute
facts.claim: Our Kicker entry: over the previous day's high, or the day-one 30-minute opening range break.

facts.quote: or the day-1 30-minute opening-range break
facts.claim: The Kicker's second entry is the day-one 30-minute opening-range break.

walkthroughs.title: What FOMO is
steps: FOMO is the fear of missing out. Everyone feels it, in markets and out of them.
In trading it's the urge to get into a move you're watching from the sidelines.
It often shows up in two ways. You buy late, after the move. Or you jump in before your signal.

walkthroughs.title: What a chase costs
steps: Your stop sits where the idea is wrong. Buy higher and you're further from it.
Risk per share is entry minus stop. Every dollar you chase gets added to it.
Keep your size and you risk more than you planned. Keep your risk and you buy fewer shares.

walkthroughs.title: The cure
steps: Write the entry and the stop before the open, while you're calm.
If you miss it, wait for a pullback that holds a higher low. Then buy with a close stop.
Or let it go. Another setup will come along.

questions.q: In trading, what is FOMO?
choices: Fear of being left out of a move
Fear of losing money on a trade
Fear of buying a stock at a high
Fear of holding a trade overnight
questions.answer: Fear of being left out of a move
questions.why: Fear of being left out of a move. FOMO is the feeling that something exciting is happening while you sit on the sidelines, and its urgency drives impulsive decisions.
questions.lesson_line: FOMO wants you in now, on somebody else's move.

wrong.Fear of losing money on a trade: That's the fear of loss. FOMO is the fear of being left out of a gain.
wrong.Fear of buying a stock at a high: That's closer to the opposite. FOMO pulls you into buying high, not away from it.
wrong.Fear of holding a trade overnight: That's worry about a gap in a trade you own. FOMO is about a move you're not in.

questions.q: Chasing is jumping into a move after it has already happened.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A chase is a position taken too late to properly benefit, sometimes right when the move is ready to reverse.
questions.lesson_line: If the move already ran without you, paying up for it is a chase.

questions.q: FOMO can also make you buy too early, before your setup gives its signal.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Steenbarger describes a trader who front-ran his setups, getting in before the proper signal. A good candidate is no reason to buy before it triggers.
questions.lesson_line: Getting in before your own signal is FOMO too. Let the trigger pull you in.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits.
questions.sentence: In an uptrend, each pullback stops above the last pullback's bottom. That's a higher ___.
questions.answer: low
questions.why: Low. An uptrend is a series of higher highs and higher lows. A pullback that holds above the last low is a higher low.
questions.lesson_line: Higher highs and higher lows. That's what an uptrend is made of.

questions.q: You buy well above your planned entry but keep the same stop. What changes?
choices: Your risk per share gets bigger
Nothing, the stop still caps the loss
The stop gets more room, so it's safer
Your upside to the target grows
questions.answer: Your risk per share gets bigger
questions.why: Your risk per share gets bigger. Risk per share is entry minus stop, so a higher entry means more lost per share if the stop is hit.
questions.lesson_line: Every dollar you chase gets added to your risk per share.

wrong.Nothing, the stop still caps the loss: The stop sets your exit price, not your loss per share. A higher entry adds to the distance down to it.
wrong.The stop gets more room, so it's safer: More room is more loss per share. The stop sits where it always did; you just paid more.
wrong.Your upside to the target grows: The other way round. A higher entry leaves less room to the same target.

questions.q: Buying strength is the same thing as chasing.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Rhodes' rule is to buy what is showing strength. A chase is getting in too late, after the move. IBD's test is how far past the buy point you get in.
questions.lesson_line: Buying strength at your trigger is a plan. Buying it far past the trigger is a chase.

questions.q: Why write your entry and stop down before the market opens?
choices: So you decide before emotions kick in
So you never take a losing trade
So a fast move can't leave you behind
questions.answer: So you decide before emotions kick in
questions.why: So you decide before emotions kick in. Fidelity: set your entries and exits in advance so you aren't making spur-of-the-moment choices at peaks or valleys.
questions.lesson_line: Make the decision while you're calm. Then just follow it.

wrong.So you never take a losing trade: A plan still has losses. It keeps them small: stick to the plan and take small losses quickly.
wrong.So a fast move can't leave you behind: You'll still miss moves. The plan stops you from chasing the ones you miss.

questions.q: Plan: buy at $30, stop at $29. You chase it to $33, same stop. Your risk per share is how many times the plan's?
questions.why: 4 times. Risk per share is entry minus stop. The stop at $29 was a dollar under $30, and it's four dollars under $33.
questions.lesson_line: Chasing doesn't move your stop. It moves your risk.

questions.q: Everyone around you is buying a stock. That alone is a good reason for you to buy it.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Others buying doesn't mean you have to. The SEC warns that following the crowd can lead to significant losses.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd buying is a feeling, not a setup.

questions.story: Your plan is to buy a break over $25.40. The stock is at $25.10 and climbing fast. You're scared it'll go without you.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Wait for $25.40, buy stop ready
Buy now before it gets away
Buy now, $25.10 is close enough
questions.answer: Wait for $25.40, buy stop ready
questions.why: Wait for $25.40 with a buy stop ready. A buy stop just over the level fills only if the break happens. Buying before the signal is FOMO too.
questions.lesson_line: Let the trigger pull you in. If it never triggers, you never needed it.

wrong.Buy now before it gets away: That's jumping ahead of the setup: in before the signal, on fear. If the break fails, you own a stock that never triggered.
wrong.Buy now, $25.10 is close enough: Close isn't the signal. The level is there because the break over it is the setup.

questions.story: You planned 200 shares at $40 with a stop at $38. That's $400 at risk. The stock opens at $43, and you buy the 200 shares anyway.
questions.q: Same stop. What is really at risk now?
questions.why: $1,000. Risk is shares times entry minus stop: 200 shares from $43 down to $38. That's more than double the $400 you planned.
questions.lesson_line: Same size, higher entry, same stop: more risk than you signed up for.

wrong.$400: That was the plan at $40. Buying higher with the same stop raised the risk on every share.
wrong.$600: That's only the extra you paid above $40. The stop is still at $38, below your old entry too.
wrong.$8,600: That's the whole position. You'd only lose all of it if the stock went to zero.

questions.q: A chat room says "get in now, this won't last." That urgency is a good reason to act fast.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Urgency is the tool. The SEC warns that scammers say an opportunity won't last to pressure you, and says never feel pressured to invest right away.
questions.lesson_line: Urgency is someone else's plan for your money. Slow down.

questions.q: On our Kicker setup, what's the day-one entry besides a break of the prior day's high?
choices: The 30-minute opening range break
The first trade at the opening bell
The close of the first day
Any dip below the open price
questions.answer: The 30-minute opening range break
questions.why: The 30-minute opening range break. Our Kicker entry is over the previous day's high, or the day-one break of the 30-minute opening range. A level triggers the buy, not the urge.
questions.lesson_line: Even on a hot gap, a level does the buying, not the urge.

wrong.The first trade at the opening bell: That's buying the urge at the bell. Our rule waits for the opening range to break.
wrong.The close of the first day: Some setups buy the close, but our Kicker entries are the prior day's high or the 30-minute range break.
wrong.Any dip below the open price: A dip under the open is not our trigger. The Kicker buys a break up through a level.

questions.q: The buy point was $40. You missed it, and the stock now trades at $43.60. How far past the buy point is it, in percent?
questions.why: 9%. That's $43.60 minus $40, divided by $40. IBD talks of a 5% buy zone after a breakout, so this is well past it.
questions.lesson_line: Measure how far past the buy point you are before you buy. Further past, more shakeout risk.

questions.story: You planned to buy the breakout over $40, stop $37. You got busy and missed it. It now trades at $44, and you feel sick about it.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Wait for a pullback, higher low
Buy now with the old stop at $37
Buy now with a stop at $43
Buy double size to catch up
questions.answer: Wait for a pullback, higher low
questions.why: Wait for a pullback and a higher low. Rhodes' rule: if a trade is missed, wait for a correction before putting it on. Buying now out of regret is how late entries get caught near a peak.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the break: let it go, or wait for the pullback. Don't buy your regret.

wrong.Buy now with the old stop at $37: That's the old stop with a much higher entry. Your risk per share more than doubles.
wrong.Buy now with a stop at $43: That stop is picked to make the chase fit, not set where the idea is wrong. Chasers get whipsawed and stopped out a lot.
wrong.Buy double size to catch up: Size can't fix a late entry. It just makes the chase bigger.

questions.q: A trader's win rate drops on the days he trades most. What does coach Brett Steenbarger often find behind it?
choices: The extra trades are FOMO trades
Busy days are just harder markets
He needs a faster trading platform
His position size was too small
questions.answer: The extra trades are FOMO trades
questions.why: The extra trades are FOMO trades. Steenbarger sees win rates fall as trade counts rise, often because the added trades come from a FOMO mindset. The fear of missing leads to marginal trades.
questions.lesson_line: When your trade count jumps, check how many came from FOMO.

wrong.Busy days are just harder markets: Some may be, but the pattern he finds is in the trader: the added trades are the marginal ones.
wrong.He needs a faster trading platform: Speed doesn't fix the choice to take a marginal trade.
wrong.His position size was too small: Size doesn't change how often trades win. The extra trades were the weak ones.

questions.story: A stock you've watched gaps up 8% at the open on news. It's 9:32 and still running. You have no entry or stop planned.
questions.q: What's the disciplined move?
choices: Wait for the opening range to set
Buy at market before it runs away
Buy now, set a stop later
Short it, the gap is far too big
questions.answer: Wait for the opening range to set
questions.why: Wait for the opening range to form. ChartSchool's gap rule gives the open an hour to set its range, and some traders watch only a few minutes. Then you have a level to buy over and a low for the stop.
questions.lesson_line: No plan, no trade. Let the range form, then buy the break with a stop under it.

wrong.Buy at market before it runs away: That's buying on urgency with no stop. The SEC's line: never feel pressured to invest right away.
wrong.Buy now, set a stop later: Without a stop you don't know your risk, so you can't size the trade.
wrong.Short it, the gap is far too big: A big gap is no reason to fight it. With no plan, the answer is to wait, not to flip sides.

questions.q: Investopedia's GameStop case: it topped at $120.75, then traded at $10.97 a few weeks later. How far down was a buyer at the top?
questions.why: 91%. That's $120.75 minus $10.97, divided by $120.75. The run came on social media hype, and many who arrived late endured significant pain.
questions.lesson_line: When the hype is everywhere, you're probably late. Late buyers take the worst of the fall.

questions.story: A stock is all over your feeds. It's up 40% in five days, and friends are posting their gains. You don't own any.
questions.q: What's the honest read?
choices: I'm late; wait for a real setup
The buzz proves it goes higher
Buy now, add more as it rises
Short it, it has to fall now
questions.answer: I'm late; wait for a real setup
questions.why: You're late. Once everyone is talking about a stock, it has likely already run, and early buyers may be ready to take profits. Wait for a real setup with a stop.
questions.lesson_line: If the whole internet knows, you're not early.

wrong.The buzz proves it goes higher: Buzz is the crowd, not a signal. The SEC warns following the crowd can lead to significant losses.
wrong.Buy now, add more as it rises: That's chasing twice. Adding to a chase just makes the chase bigger.
wrong.Short it, it has to fall now: A fast run can keep running. Shorting it with no setup is a guess, not a plan.

questions.q: Yesterday's low was $48.50. Today it opens up 8% at $54. With our default stop at yesterday's low, how far away is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 10.2%. That's $54 minus $48.50, divided by $54. Our default stop is the day's low or the prior day's low, and after a big gap the prior low is far away. The same risk buys far fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: After a gap, measure the stop before you buy. A wide stop means a small position.

questions.story: Your journal shows a pattern. You miss your planned entry, then chase the move. Most of those trades end as small stop-outs.
questions.q: What fix goes at the root?
choices: Grade each day on following the plan
Trade more names so you miss less
Use wider stops on the chases
Buy before the signal to beat it
questions.answer: Grade each day on following the plan
questions.why: Grade each day on following the plan. Steenbarger's client chased moves that ran from his entry and took paper-cut losses. He graded himself each day purely on process.
questions.lesson_line: Score your day on the process, not the P&L.

wrong.Trade more names so you miss less: More names means more chances to chase. You'll always miss moves; the job is the best ones.
wrong.Use wider stops on the chases: A wider stop on a chase is more risk on a worse entry.
wrong.Buy before the signal to beat it: That's FOMO's other face: in before the signal, on fear.

questions.q: Missing a trade costs you money, just like taking a loss.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. A missed trade takes nothing out of your account; you give up a possible gain. Steenbarger: the danger in missing is not financial, it's the self-criticism after. Rhodes: not having a position is a position.
questions.lesson_line: A missed trade leaves your account whole. A chased trade can cost plenty.

questions.story: You missed the breakout over $40. It ran to $45, then pulled back to $41, above its last low, and turned up.
questions.q: You buy the turn near $41, stop just under the pullback low. Is it a chase?
choices: No, it's a pullback near support
Yes, it already broke out at $40
Yes, only new highs are safe
questions.answer: No, it's a pullback near support
questions.why: No. Broken resistance usually turns into support on pullbacks, and the best place to buy is near support. The pullback held a higher low, and your stop sits just under it.
questions.lesson_line: Miss the break, wait for the pullback that holds. That's your second chance.

wrong.Yes, it already broke out at $40: A breakout you missed isn't gone. Rhodes: if a trade is missed, wait for a correction, then put it on. That's this.
wrong.Yes, only new highs are safe: Buying near support with a close stop is the spot Murphy calls best. A new high far from support means a wider stop.

questions.story: You've chased three moves this week and been stopped out of all three. Another stock is ripping, and you feel the pull again.
questions.q: What do you do right now?
choices: Step back; no trade until calm
Buy, this one will make it back
Go in with double the size
Enter, but with a very tight stop
questions.answer: Step back; no trade until calm
questions.why: Step back. ChartSchool's advice: when emotions run high, take a breather and step back. Schwab: if you can't separate emotions from decisions, slow down or take a break.
questions.lesson_line: When you feel the pull this hard, step away from the screen.

wrong.Buy, this one will make it back: That's trading to win money back, not trading a setup. Rhodes says don't give in to that urge.
wrong.Go in with double the size: Doubling size on a FOMO trade doubles the damage if it's another chase.
wrong.Enter, but with a very tight stop: A tight stop on a chase often gets whipsawed. Steenbarger sees chasers stopped out often.

questions.q: The goal is to catch as many of the big moves as you can.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Nobody takes every opportunity; the job is limiting risk and taking the best ones. ChartSchool: being consistently profitable matters more than chasing movers.
questions.lesson_line: You'll miss plenty of moves. Your job is the best few, done well.
